edbDesc: A method of strengthening materials by changing their average crystallite (grain) size. It is based on the observation that grain boundaries impede dislocation movement and that the number of dislocations within a grain have an effect on how easily dislocations can traverse grain boundaries and travel from grain to grain. Changing grain size can influence dislocation movement and yield strength.
title: Grain-boundary strengthening
description: Metal made of smaller crystal grains is stronger, because the boundaries between grains block the slipping that lets metal bend. Eric Hall (1951) and Norman Petch (1953) worked out the rule; steelmakers now roll and cool steel carefully to keep the grains tiny.
effect: smaller crystal grains make a metal stronger
usedIn: High-strength low-alloy steel in car bodies
strength: Shrinking the grains from about 0.1 mm to 0.01 mm roughly doubles the strength of mild steel, without adding any alloy.
pickWhy: A specific, named metallurgical effect (Hall-Petch) that does a clear job and is not in the deck.
